prompt:
Write a technical description of about 800 words of how Git stores a commit, covering blobs, trees, commit objects and refs. The reader is a developer who uses Git every day and has never looked inside the .git directory.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

text:
When you run git commit, the result is a small set of files in the .git/objects directory, and it helps to know that Git is, at its core, a content-addressable filesystem. You hand it a piece of content, it computes a SHA-1 hash of that content (newer repositories can use SHA-256), and it stores the content under a path derived from that hash. The hash is the name. Identical content always produces the identical name, and changing even one byte produces a completely different one. Everything else in Git, including branches, history and merges, is built on top of this idea using only four kinds of object: blobs, trees, commits and tags. The first three are what a normal commit involves.

A blob holds the contents of a single file and nothing more. It has no filename, no permissions and no timestamp. When Git stores a blob, it prepends a short header consisting of the word blob, a space, the size in bytes and a null byte, hashes the header and content together, compresses the result with zlib and writes it to .git/objects. The first two hex characters of the hash become a directory name and the remaining thirty-eight become the filename, so an object with hash ab12cd... lives at .git/objects/ab/12cd.... Because the name depends only on the content, two files in your project with identical contents share one blob, and a file that is unchanged between commits costs nothing extra. You can see this for yourself with git cat-file -p followed by a hash, which decompresses and prints the object, and git cat-file -t, which tells you its type.

If blobs have no names, something else must record which blob is which file, and that is the job of a tree. A tree represents a single directory. It is a list of entries, and each entry holds a file mode (such as 100644 for a regular file, 100755 for an executable, or 040000 for a subdirectory), a name and the hash of the object it points to. For a regular file that hash refers to a blob, and for a subdirectory it refers to another tree. A repository with nested folders therefore becomes a tree of trees, with the root tree describing the top level of your project and its leaves being blobs. Since a tree is itself hashed by its contents, and those contents include the hashes of its children, a change to one deeply nested file changes that blob's hash, which changes its parent tree's hash, and so on up to the root. This is a Merkle tree, and it means a single root hash identifies the exact state of every file in the project. It also means that when you change one file, Git only needs to write new objects along the path from that file to the root, while every untouched subtree is reused as it was.

The commit object is the piece that adds history and meaning. A commit is a small text object with a few lines of metadata followed by your message. The first line, tree, gives the hash of the root tree, which is the complete snapshot of the project at that moment. Next come zero or more parent lines, each naming the hash of a previous commit. A normal commit has one parent, the first commit in a repository has none, and a merge commit has two or more. Then come the author and committer lines, each with a name, an email address, a timestamp and a timezone offset, and finally a blank line and the commit message. Git hashes this text just as it does a blob, so the commit's identity depends on its snapshot, its parents, its authorship and its message. Because each commit names its parents by hash, the history forms a chain in which altering any old commit would change its hash and therefore the hash of every commit after it. This is why rewriting history, as rebase does, produces new commits rather than editing old ones.

One consequence worth noticing is that Git stores snapshots, not diffs. Each commit points at a full tree. The diffs you see in git log -p or in a pull request are computed on demand by comparing two trees. To save disk space Git does eventually pack objects together, and in packfiles it does store similar objects as deltas against each other, but that is an optimisation hidden beneath the model. Conceptually, every commit is a complete picture of the project.

All of those objects are immutable and identified by long hashes, which are not much use for day-to-day work, and refs are what make the system usable. A ref is a human-friendly name that points at a hash. A branch is nothing more than a file under .git/refs/heads containing the forty-character hash of a commit. If you open .git/refs/heads/main in a text editor, you will see exactly that. Tags live under .git/refs/tags in the same way, and remote-tracking branches such as origin/main live under .git/refs/remotes. Making a commit moves the current branch's file to contain the new commit's hash, and that is the whole meaning of a branch advancing. Branches are cheap precisely because creating one just writes forty characters to a file.

Finally, Git needs to know which branch you are on, and it records that in .git/HEAD. Normally this file contains a symbolic reference such as ref: refs/heads/main, meaning HEAD follows the main branch. When you check out a specific commit directly, HEAD instead contains a raw hash, which is the detached HEAD state. So a commit in Git is a blob per file, trees tying names to blobs, a commit object tying a root tree to its parents and message, and a ref pointing at the newest commit.
